questions.stem: Which pathogen is classified as a macroorganism?
options: Staphylococcus aureus
Tapeworm
Plasmodium
Influenza virus
questions.explanation: Macroorganisms, or macroparasites, are multicellular and visible without a microscope, such as tapeworms, ticks and lice. Plasmodium is a single-celled protozoan, a microorganism.

questions.stem: Which infectious agents are non-cellular?
options: Prions and protozoans
Viruses and prions
Bacteria and fungi
Protozoans and viruses
questions.explanation: Viruses are genetic material in a protein coat, and prions are misfolded proteins; neither is made of cells. Bacteria, fungi and protozoans are all cellular microorganisms.

questions.stem: What feature allows prions to cause disease?
options: They release toxins that destroy the myelin sheath around nerve cells
They are misfolded proteins that make normal ones misfold too
They contain DNA that takes over the host cell's ribosomes to make new prions
They reproduce by binary fission inside nerve cells of the brain
questions.explanation: A prion is an abnormally folded form of a normal brain protein; when it contacts the normal form it converts it, so misfolded proteins build up and damage nerve tissue. Prions have no DNA or RNA.

questions.stem: Surgical instruments used on a patient with Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease need special treatment, because normal sterilisation may not destroy prions. Why are prions so resistant?
options: They are protected by a thick cell wall made of peptidoglycan and lipids
They form endospores that survive boiling and long periods of dry conditions
They are wrapped in a lipid envelope that repels water and disinfectants
Their misfolded structure resists heat and protein-digesting enzymes
questions.explanation: The misfolded prion protein forms stable clumps that are not broken down by normal autoclaving or by proteases. Prions are not cells, so they have no cell wall, envelope or spores.

questions.stem: Which feature helps a virus to enter its host cells?
options: Flagella that drive it through the mucus to reach the host cells
A cell wall that resists being broken down by lysozyme
Hooks and suckers that attach it firmly to the gut wall
Surface proteins that bind receptors on host cell membranes
questions.explanation: Viral surface proteins fit particular receptor molecules, which decides which cells and species a virus can infect. Viruses have no flagella or cell walls, and hooks are a feature of macroparasites such as tapeworms.

questions.stem: Which adaptation helps some bacteria survive harsh conditions outside a host?
options: Forming endospores
Forming hyphae
Having a protein capsid
Having a hooked scolex
questions.explanation: Endospores are dormant, tough-walled structures that survive heat, drying and chemicals, as in the tetanus bacterium in soil. Hyphae belong to fungi, capsids to viruses and scolices to tapeworms.

questions.stem: Plasmodium, the protozoan that causes malaria, spends part of its life cycle inside human red blood cells. How does this help it?
options: It is protected from the mosquito's digestive enzymes there
It is hidden inside host cells, where antibodies cannot reach it
It uses the iron in haemoglobin to photosynthesise inside the cell
It gains a protective cell wall from the red blood cell membrane
questions.explanation: Inside red blood cells and liver cells, Plasmodium is shielded from antibodies in the plasma, and red blood cells do not display antigens to T cells the way most cells do. Plasmodium is not photosynthetic.

questions.stem: How are the fungi that cause tinea (athlete's foot) adapted to infect the skin?
options: They swim through sweat using flagella to reach the bloodstream
They are misfolded proteins that convert the keratin in skin
Their hyphae secrete enzymes that digest keratin in skin
They inject their DNA into skin cells, which then make new fungi
questions.explanation: Tinea fungi grow as hyphae through the dead outer layer of skin and secrete enzymes that break down keratin for food. Injecting genetic material into cells is how viruses infect.

questions.stem: A tick can feed on a host's blood for several days without being noticed. Which adaptation helps it do this?
options: A protein capsid that hides it from the host's antibodies and white blood cells
Endospores that let it survive in the blood without being attacked or digested
Surface proteins that let it enter the host's red blood cells and hide inside
Saliva containing anticoagulants and substances that reduce pain and inflammation
questions.explanation: Tick saliva stops blood clotting and suppresses local pain and immune responses, so the tick stays attached and unnoticed. Capsids belong to viruses, and ticks are external macroparasites.

questions.stem: Which is an example of vector transmission?
options: Cholera spread by drinking contaminated water
Dengue virus carried between people by Aedes mosquitoes
Influenza spread by touching a contaminated door handle
Cold sores spread by kissing an infected person
questions.explanation: A vector is a living organism, often an insect, that carries a pathogen from one host to another; dengue is spread by Aedes mosquitoes. Door handles and water are non-living, so they give indirect transmission.

questions.stem: A child catches a cold after touching a toy that an infected child had sneezed on, and then rubbing her eyes. Which type of transmission is this?
options: Indirect contact through a contaminated object
Direct contact with the infected person
Vector transmission by an animal carrier
Vertical transmission from mother to child
questions.explanation: The virus passed via a non-living object, called a fomite, so this is indirect contact. Direct contact would require touching the infected person, and a vector is a living carrier.

questions.stem: Paper discs soaked in different antimicrobial solutions are placed on agar spread with bacteria from a water sample. What is measured to compare the antimicrobials?
options: The colour of the bacterial colonies under each disc
The temperature of the agar plate after incubation
The number of discs still attached to the agar
The diameter of the clear zone around each disc
questions.explanation: Where the antimicrobial diffuses out and stops growth, a clear zone of inhibition forms; a wider zone generally means a more effective substance at that concentration.

questions.stem: In the antimicrobial disc investigation, what is the best control?
options: A disc soaked in the bacterial culture
A plate left with no bacteria spread on it
A disc soaked in sterile water
A disc soaked in the strongest antimicrobial
questions.explanation: A disc soaked in sterile water, the solvent, shows that any clear zone is due to the antimicrobial and not to the disc itself. A plate with no bacteria would not show anything about the discs.

questions.stem: In school investigations, agar plates are taped closed and incubated at about 25 to 30 degrees Celsius rather than at 37 degrees Celsius. Why?
options: Because antimicrobial substances work only at temperatures below 30 degrees Celsius
Because bacteria from food and water cannot grow at all at human body temperature
To make the clear zones around the discs dry out and become visible more quickly
To limit microbes adapted to the human body, which are likelier to be pathogens
questions.explanation: Microbes that thrive at body temperature are more likely to cause human disease, so a lower temperature reduces risk; taping stops the plates being opened. Many food and water bacteria can grow at 37 degrees Celsius, which is the reason for caution.

questions.stem: Samples of a non-pathogenic E. coli culture are heated to different temperatures for 10 minutes and then plated. Fewer colonies grow from samples heated to higher temperatures. What is the best explanation?
options: High temperatures denature bacterial proteins, killing more of the cells
High temperatures speed up reproduction, so colonies merge and are hard to count
High temperatures turn E. coli into endospores that cannot form visible colonies
High temperatures remove the nutrients from the agar before colonies can form
questions.explanation: Each colony grows from a surviving cell, so fewer colonies means fewer viable cells; heat denatures enzymes and other proteins and kills bacteria. E. coli does not form endospores, and the agar is added after heating.

questions.stem: Which statement distinguishes the innate immune response from the adaptive response?
options: Innate responses are non-specific and fast; adaptive responses are specific and form memory
Innate responses are specific and form memory; adaptive responses are non-specific and fast
Innate responses happen only in plants; adaptive responses happen only in animals
Innate responses use antibodies; adaptive responses use only phagocytes and fever
questions.explanation: Innate defences act the same way against any pathogen and respond within minutes to hours. The adaptive response targets one specific antigen, takes days the first time, and leaves memory cells.

questions.stem: Which is part of the first line of defence against pathogens?
options: Hydrochloric acid secreted in the stomach
Antibodies released by plasma cells
Phagocytes engulfing bacteria in tissues
Fever raising the body's temperature
questions.explanation: The first line consists of barriers and their secretions, such as skin, mucus, tears and stomach acid, which stop pathogens entering. Phagocytes and fever are second-line innate responses, and antibodies belong to the adaptive response.

questions.stem: Neutrophils and macrophages are phagocytic leukocytes. What do they do?
options: Kill infected body cells by releasing perforin onto their surface
Release histamine to make nearby blood vessels widen and leak
Engulf pathogens and digest them with enzymes inside the cell
Secrete antibodies that are specific to one particular antigen
questions.explanation: Phagocytes take in pathogens by phagocytosis, and lysosomes fuse with the vesicle to digest them. Antibodies come from plasma cells, perforin from cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells, and histamine from mast cells.

questions.stem: Which pairing of an antimicrobial protein and its action is correct?
options: Antibody: digests bacteria after they have been engulfed by a phagocyte
Complement: bursts bacteria and tags them for phagocytes
Interferon: breaks down bacterial cell walls in tears and saliva
Lysozyme: warns nearby cells that a virus is infecting the tissue
questions.explanation: Complement proteins in plasma can form pores that burst bacteria and coat them so phagocytes engulf them more easily. Interferons warn nearby cells of viral infection, and lysozyme breaks down bacterial cell walls.

questions.stem: Why does an area of inflammation become red and warm?
options: Histamine widens blood vessels, increasing blood flow to the area
Pathogens give off heat as they reproduce rapidly in the tissue
Antibodies collect in the area and absorb red light from the skin
Phagocytes release a red pigment when they digest the bacteria
questions.explanation: Mast cells release histamine, which dilates blood vessels and makes them leakier, so more warm blood reaches the area and fluid and phagocytes move into the tissue. The heat comes from the extra blood, not the pathogens.

questions.stem: How does fever help the body fight an infection?
options: A higher temperature slows pathogens and speeds immune reactions
A higher temperature denatures human enzymes, so infected cells stop working
A higher temperature kills every bacterium in the body within a few hours
A higher temperature makes antibodies divide and multiply more quickly
questions.explanation: Chemicals released during infection reset the body's temperature set point in the hypothalamus; the higher temperature is less favourable to many pathogens and speeds up immune cell activity. A fever is not high enough to denature the body's own enzymes unless it becomes extreme.

questions.stem: What is the role of interleukins in the immune response?
options: They are signals that let immune cells activate one another
They are antibodies that bind antigens on the surface of bacteria
They are enzymes in tears that break down bacterial cell walls
They are receptors on T cells that bind antigens on MHC markers
questions.explanation: Interleukins are cytokines released by white blood cells to communicate between innate and adaptive cells, for example from macrophages to helper T cells and from helper T cells to B cells and cytotoxic T cells.

questions.stem: A macrophage presents an antigen to a helper T cell and releases interleukin-1. The activated helper T cell then releases interleukin-2. What is the main effect of interleukin-2?
options: It switches off the adaptive response once the infection ends
It stimulates selected T and B cells to divide and differentiate
It makes the macrophage engulf more pathogens at the site
It binds to the antigen and neutralises the pathogen directly
questions.explanation: Interleukin-2 drives clonal expansion: T cells and B cells with receptors for that antigen multiply and become effector and memory cells. Neutralising antigens is the job of antibodies.

questions.stem: What do cytotoxic T cells do?
options: Secrete large amounts of antibodies into the blood and lymph
Engulf bacteria and debris at the site of an infection
Release histamine to start the inflammatory response
Destroy body cells infected by viruses or turned cancerous
questions.explanation: Cytotoxic T cells recognise infected or abnormal cells displaying a foreign antigen on MHC markers and kill them, for example with perforin. Antibodies are secreted by plasma cells.

questions.stem: What is the role of suppressor (regulatory) T cells?
options: They activate B cells so that they begin to produce antibodies
They destroy body cells that are infected by intracellular pathogens
They store a record of the antigen for any future infection
They dampen the immune response once an infection is under control
questions.explanation: Suppressor T cells, now usually called regulatory T cells, slow and stop the response when it is no longer needed and help prevent attacks on the body's own cells. Activating B cells is the role of helper T cells.

questions.stem: HIV destroys helper T cells. Why does this weaken both the humoral and the cell-mediated responses?
options: Helper T cells are the only cells in the body that are able to make antibodies
Helper T cells are the phagocytes that engulf and destroy all invading pathogens
Helper T cells form the mucous membranes that act as the body's first barrier
Helper T cells release interleukins that activate B and cytotoxic T cells
questions.explanation: Most B cell and cytotoxic T cell responses need signals from helper T cells, so losing them leaves both arms of the adaptive response weak. Antibodies are made by plasma cells, not helper T cells.

questions.stem: After recovery from a viral infection, which cells allow a faster cell-mediated response if the same virus returns?
options: Neutrophils
Mast cells
Memory T cells
Plasma cells
questions.explanation: Memory T cells formed during the first response persist for years and multiply quickly on a second exposure. Plasma cells belong to the humoral response, and neutrophils and mast cells are innate.

questions.stem: During the humoral response, what do activated B cells differentiate into?
options: Macrophages and neutrophils, which engulf the pathogen
Mast cells, which release histamine, and memory B cells
Plasma cells, which secrete antibodies, and memory B cells
Cytotoxic T cells and helper T cells, which attack infected cells
questions.explanation: A selected B cell divides into a clone of plasma cells, which release large amounts of antibody, and long-lived memory B cells. T cells mature from different precursors in the thymus.

questions.stem: How do antibodies help to eliminate bacteria in the body's fluids?
options: They kill infected body cells by releasing perforin onto their membranes
They raise the body's temperature, which stops bacteria from reproducing
They bind antigens, clumping bacteria together and marking them for phagocytes
They enter the bacterial cells and digest the bacterial DNA from the inside
questions.explanation: Antibodies bind specific antigens, causing agglutination, neutralising toxins and coating bacteria so phagocytes recognise and engulf them. Perforin is released by cytotoxic T cells.

questions.stem: A graph shows antibody levels after two exposures to the same antigen. After the first, antibodies appear after about 10 days and peak at a low level. After the second, they appear within 2 to 3 days and peak far higher. What explains the second response?
options: The antigen was weaker at the second exposure, so it was easier to fight
Innate defences became specific to the antigen after the first exposure
Memory B cells from the first response quickly produce many plasma cells
Antibodies left from the first response multiplied rapidly in the blood
questions.explanation: Memory B cells are already selected for the antigen, so on re-exposure they divide into plasma cells far faster and in larger numbers. Antibodies are proteins and cannot multiply.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows the cell-mediated response on first exposure to a virus?
options: Plasma cells release antibodies; helper T cells activated; antigen presented; memory T cells remain
Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells; antigen presented; helper T cells activated; memory B cells remain
Memory T cells multiply; antigen presented; plasma cells release antibodies; infected cells killed
Antigen presented; helper T cells activated; cytotoxic T cells multiply; infected cells killed; memory T cells remain
questions.explanation: An antigen-presenting cell shows the viral antigen to helper T cells, which release interleukins that drive clonal expansion of matching cytotoxic T cells; these kill infected cells, and memory T cells remain. Plasma cells and antibodies belong to the humoral response.

questions.stem: Which is an example of artificial active immunity?
options: Receiving antibodies in breast milk
Receiving an injection of antivenom
Making antibodies after catching chickenpox
Making antibodies after a vaccine injection
questions.explanation: Active immunity means the person's own immune system makes antibodies and memory cells; artificial means it was triggered deliberately, as by a vaccine. Catching chickenpox gives natural active immunity, and antivenom gives passive immunity.

questions.stem: Why does passive immunity give only short-term protection?
options: The person's own B cells destroy the donated antibodies within an hour
No memory cells form, and the donated antibodies are gradually broken down
The donated antibodies multiply too fast and begin to attack the body
Passive immunity works against bacteria but never against viruses
questions.explanation: The antibodies come ready-made from another source, so the recipient's own B cells are not activated and no memory forms; the antibodies are broken down over weeks to months.

questions.stem: How does a vaccine prepare the adaptive immune system?
options: It kills any pathogens already present in the body's tissues
It strengthens the skin and mucous membranes against entry
It presents antigens without causing disease, so memory cells form
It supplies ready-made antibodies that stay in the blood for life
questions.explanation: A vaccine contains antigens, as weakened or inactivated pathogens, parts of them or instructions to make them, which trigger a primary response and leave memory cells. A later infection then meets a fast secondary response.

questions.stem: In a country, measles notifications fell by more than 95% in the decade after a two-dose vaccination program began, as coverage rose above 90%. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The data prove that measles has been eradicated from every country in the world
The data show that the vaccine protects adults but has little effect on children
The vaccine program most likely caused the fall, as cases dropped as coverage rose
The fall was caused by measles virus becoming a milder disease in those ten years
questions.explanation: The fall in cases follows the rise in coverage and is very large, which supports the vaccine as the cause; comparing vaccinated and unvaccinated groups would strengthen this. Data from one country say nothing about the rest of the world.

questions.stem: Why are antibiotics ineffective against viral infections such as colds?
options: Antibiotics destroy the white blood cells that normally fight viruses
Viruses make antibiotics of their own that cancel out the drug
Viruses lack the cell walls and ribosomes that antibiotics target
Viruses are too large for antibiotic molecules to get inside them
questions.explanation: Antibiotics act on bacterial structures such as cell walls and bacterial ribosomes. Viruses use the host cell's machinery, so they offer no such targets; antiviral drugs act on specific viral steps instead.

questions.stem: Oseltamivir treats influenza by blocking neuraminidase, an enzyme new virus particles need to escape from infected cells. How does this compare with penicillin?
options: Both drugs kill the pathogen by breaking down the cell wall that surrounds it
The antiviral destroys viral DNA directly; penicillin destroys bacterial ribosomes
Both drugs work by stimulating the patient's B cells to make more antibodies
The antiviral stops virus release from cells; penicillin blocks cell wall building
questions.explanation: Neuraminidase inhibitors trap new virus particles on the infected cell, limiting spread, while penicillin blocks synthesis of the bacterial cell wall so bacteria burst. Influenza has an RNA genome and no cell wall.

questions.stem: Which pair of measures is aimed mainly at indirect contact transmission?
options: Draining water and screening windows
Cleaning surfaces and washing hands
Mosquito control and insect repellent
Vaccination and antiviral medication
questions.explanation: Indirect transmission occurs through contaminated objects, food or water, so cleaning surfaces and hand washing break that route. Mosquito control, repellent, draining water and screens target vectors.

questions.stem: What is the difference between quarantine and isolation?
options: Quarantine separates people who may have been exposed; isolation separates the infected
Isolation separates people who may have been exposed; quarantine separates the infected
Quarantine applies only to animals and plants; isolation applies only to people
Quarantine treats infected people with drugs; isolation gives them vaccinations
questions.explanation: Quarantine restricts the movement of people who have been exposed but are not known to be sick, in case they develop the disease, while isolation separates people known to be infected. Both limit transmission.
